chapter.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why

cards.body:
In 399 BC a jury of about 500 Athenians voted to kill a 70-year-old man whose only weapon was a question. Socrates wrote nothing; he stood in the market and asked people what their big words meant, courage, justice, piety, and kept asking until the answers ran out.

At the long dinner table he is the first guest, and the one who **won't let anyone leave until they've explained what they just said.**
cards.simpler:
In 399 BC, about 500 people in Athens voted to put a 70-year-old man to death. His only weapon was a question. Socrates never wrote a book. He stood in the market and asked people what their big words meant, like courage or fairness, and kept asking until they ran out of answers.

At our long dinner table he is the first guest, the one who **won't let anyone leave until they've explained what they just said.**

cards.prompt: A general tells Socrates: 'Courage is standing your ground in battle.' Socrates asks: 'And the cavalry who retreat, then wheel round and win? Cowards?' What is Socrates doing?

options.text: Proving the general is a coward
Finding one case the definition doesn't fit, so the general has to think again
Showing that courage doesn't really exist

whyNot.a: That's an insult, not a question: Socrates goes after the sentence, never the man.
whyNot.c: That's the conclusion people fear, not the one he draws: a definition that fails doesn't make the thing unreal, it means we haven't pinned it yet.

cards.reteach: Socrates takes a confident sentence and holds one real case against it. If the case doesn't fit, the sentence was too small. The general isn't wrong about courage; he's wrong about having finished thinking about it.

cards.title: Ask until it runs out
cards.body:
The method is short. Find someone sure of something. Ask 'what do you mean by that?' Take their answer and test it against one real case. Ask again. Philosophers call this *elenchus*, a Greek word for cross-examination, but it's really just not letting go.

By the third or fourth question most people have nothing left. **That empty spot is the point.** Before it, they were repeating; after it, they're thinking.

It works like tapping along a wall to find the hollow part. The sound changes. Socrates said the one thing he knew was that he knew nothing, and he meant it as a tool, not an apology.
cards.simpler:
The method is short. Find someone sure of something. Ask what they mean. Test the answer on one real case. Ask again. By question three or four, most people have nothing left. **That empty spot is the point.** Before it they were repeating. After it they are thinking.

It's like tapping a wall to find the hollow part. Socrates said the only thing he knew was that he knew nothing. He meant that as a tool, not an apology.

cards.title: Euthyphro has somewhere to be
cards.body: Outside the Athens court, a man named Euthyphro tells Socrates he is prosecuting his own father for murder, and he is certain the gods approve. Socrates asks what 'approved by the gods' means. Euthyphro: 'Whatever the gods love.' Socrates points out the gods quarrel constantly, and anyway, do they love a thing because it's right, or is it right because they love it? Four tries later, **Euthyphro remembers he's in a hurry** and walks off. Plato wrote the whole exchange down; it still ends with nobody knowing what piety is.
cards.simpler: Outside the Athens court, Euthyphro tells Socrates he is prosecuting his own father for murder. He is sure the gods approve. Socrates asks what that means. Euthyphro says: whatever the gods love. But the gods argue constantly, Socrates says. Do they love a thing because it is right, or is it right because they love it? Four tries later, **Euthyphro remembers he is in a hurry** and walks off. Plato wrote it down. Nobody ever says what piety means.

cards.prompt: You believe 'hard work always pays off.' You want to run Socrates on it. Which next step is his?

options.text: Find three success stories that prove it
Look for one person who worked hard and it didn't pay off, and see what the belief does with them
Replace it with 'nothing pays off', since it's clearly not always true

whyNot.a: That's building a case for the claim, not testing it: Socrates goes looking for the case that doesn't fit.
whyNot.c: That's swapping one unexamined claim for another: a belief that fails one case needs sharpening, not flipping.

cards.reteach: The move is always the same. Say the belief out loud, then hunt for the one real case it can't explain. When you find it, the belief either shrinks or gets more precise. Either way you now know something you didn't.

cards.title: Why it got him killed
cards.body:
You'd think questions are harmless. In 399 BC Athens had just lost a long war to Sparta, and some of the men who'd wrecked the city had once sat at Socrates' feet. The charges were corrupting the young and not believing in the city's gods. He called himself a horsefly on a lazy horse, the horse being Athens. The jury voted guilty, and he drank hemlock.

One question you can't answer costs a little face. Five in a row, in the market, in front of your friends, costs a lot. **A whole city can want the horsefly gone.**

Your version is quieter. Pick a belief, ask why, answer, ask why again. Count the rounds before you say 'it just is.' That number is the depth of the belief.
cards.simpler:
Questions look harmless. But Athens had just lost a long war, and some men who wrecked the city had been Socrates' students. He was charged with corrupting the young and not believing in the city's gods. He called himself a horsefly biting the lazy horse of Athens. He was found guilty and drank poison.

One question you can't answer stings a little. Five in a row, in public, stings a lot. **A whole city can want the horsefly gone.**

cards.body: Maya tries it on her flatmate over the recycling. Six questions in, the flatmate says 'fine, you win' and goes to bed. Maya feels sharp. She has done debate, not philosophy. **The tell is that she never pointed the questions at herself.** Socrates' method finds gaps; if the only gap you ever find is in someone else, you're holding it the wrong way round.
cards.simpler: Maya tries the method on her flatmate during an argument about recycling. After six questions the flatmate says 'fine, you win' and goes to bed. Maya feels clever. But she has done debate, not philosophy. **The giveaway is that she never pointed the questions at herself.** Socrates' method is for finding gaps. If the only gaps you ever find are in other people, you are holding the tool the wrong way round.

cards.prompt: Socrates said the only thing he knew was that he knew nothing. In this chapter's terms, what did he mean?

options.text: Nothing can be known, so stop trying
He'd tapped the wall on his own beliefs too, found the hollow spots, and that's where his thinking started
He hadn't read enough books yet

whyNot.a: That's giving up, not the method: he kept asking precisely because the gap can be narrowed.
whyNot.c: That's about information, not understanding: a general can know everything about battles and still not be able to say what courage is.

cards.reteach: The empty spot where answers run out isn't a failure, it's the starting line. Socrates found it in generals and priests, but he also found it in himself, and said so. Knowing where your knowledge stops is the one piece of knowledge he claimed.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Socrates asked people what they meant, tested the answer against one real case, and kept going until the answers ran out. **That gap is where thinking starts**, and Athens killed him for finding it in public.

Tomorrow: teacher and student, 20 years together, split over whether this table is real.
cards.simpler:
Socrates asked people what they meant. He tested each answer against one real case, and kept going until the answers ran out. **That gap is where thinking starts.** Athens killed him for finding it in public.

Tomorrow: a teacher and a student, 20 years together, who split over whether this table is real.

cards.body: Tonight, say one thing you're sure of out loud. Ask 'why?' and answer. Ask again. Count the rounds before you reach 'it just is', and write that number down.
cards.simpler: Tonight, say one thing you are sure of, out loud. Ask yourself why. Answer it. Then ask why again, about the new answer. Keep going. **Count how many rounds you get through** before you reach 'it just is.' Write that number down. It tells you how deep the belief really goes.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where the answers run out.
